displayQuote: Patience is the art of hoping

meta.title: Who really said "Patience is the art of hoping"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Vauvenargues: “La patience est l’art d’espérer,” maxim 251 of his Réflexions et maximes (1746); the English wording matches Elizabeth Lee’s 1903 translation, p. 180.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Patience is the art of hoping'?
meta.ogDescription: Real, and traceable to the page. Vauvenargues wrote it in French in 1746; the four-word English sentence has been in print since at least 1880 and matches Lee’s 1903 translation word for word.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorName: Luc de Clapiers, Marquis de Vauvenargues
answer.sourceLine: He wrote it in French — “La patience est l’art d’espérer” — as one of the numbered maxims appended to Introduction à la connoissance de l’esprit humain, the single volume he published anonymously in 1746, the year before he died. The familiar four-word English sentence is a translator’s rendering, and it matches Elizabeth Lee’s 1903 translation, page 180 ↗ word for word.

source.heading: The maxim, in the book he published himself

docMeta.dd: Paris: Antoine-Claude Briasson, 1746 — appended to Introduction à la connoissance de l’esprit humain, issued anonymously
No. 251 (CCLI) in the standard later numbering
Elizabeth Lee, 1903 (Westminster: Archibald Constable & Co.), p. 180

source.excerpt: The favourites of fortune or of fame topple from their pedestals before our eyes without diverting us from ambition. — Patience is the art of hoping. — Despair puts the last touch not only to our misery but also to our weakness.
trail: 1746 — The maxim is there in the book he published in his own lifetime. The Briasson first edition of Introduction à la connoissance de l’esprit humain, suivie de Réflexions et de Maximes ↗ carries “La patience est l’art d’espérer.” among the numbered maxims of its third book.

1880 — The English sentence is already circulating in exactly its modern form. J. De Finod’s anthology A Thousand Flashes of French Wit, Wisdom, and Wickedness (New York: D. Appleton, 1880) ↗ prints “Patience is the art of hoping.” under the bare name “Vauvenargues.”

1903 — Elizabeth Lee’s La Bruyère and Vauvenargues: Selections from the Characters, Reflexions and Maxims ↗ gives the same four words on page 180. This is the edition modern quote sites are unknowingly reprinting.
1940 — F. G. Stevens’s facing-page edition ↗ sets “La patience est l’art d’espérer.” against “Patience is the art of hoping.” and places it at maxim 251, between 250 and 252.
source.excerptNote: Three maxims as they run consecutively in Elizabeth Lee’s 1903 translation. The French original of the middle one reads “La patience est l’art d’espérer.”
source.rightsNote: Both halves of this quotation are out of copyright in the United States. The French original was first published in 1746, and the English wording matches Elizabeth Lee’s translation of 1903 — with the identical sentence already in print in an American anthology of 1880. F. G. Stevens’s 1940 translation happens to render it the same way, but nothing here depends on that later edition.

author.name: Luc de Clapiers, Marquis de Vauvenargues
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.bio: Luc de Clapiers, Marquis de Vauvenargues, was born at Aix-en-Provence in 1715 and served as an infantry officer, taking part in the Siege of Prague in 1742 and the Battle of Dettingen before ill health ended his career. In 1746 he published a single anonymous volume, Introduction à la connoissance de l’esprit humain, with his Réflexions et maximes appended; Voltaire, who had been corresponding with him since 1743, urged him into print and then toward a revised edition. He died in Paris in 1747 at 31, and is now read alongside La Rochefoucauld and La Bruyère as one of the great French moralists — the warmest of the three.

misattribution.heading: What gets lost, even though the attribution is right
misattribution.intro: This one is genuine, which makes it unusual for a quote this widely shared. What travels badly is everything around it: the man’s name, the translator’s name, and the date.

items.why: Vauvenargues wrote in French, so the four-word English sentence is some translator’s work. It matches Lee’s 1903 text on p. 180 ↗ word for word — and that is the volume the quote sites name as their source, while printing no translator credit at all.

items.who: “Luc de Clapiers”, filed as though a different writer
items.why: Aggregators split one person into two entries. AZQuotes credits it simply to “Luc de Clapiers” ↗, while other sites credit “Vauvenargues”. Luc de Clapiers was the Marquis de Vauvenargues.

items.who: 1903, cited as though it were the origin
items.why: The source line AZQuotes gives is the 1903 Lee volume ↗ — which is the translation, not the work. The maxim itself dates from the 1746 edition.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the sentence are both his: the 1746 first edition ↗ has “La patience est l’art d’espérer.” The English is the standard literal rendering, identical in De Finod (1880), Lee (1903) and Stevens (1940) — it is the Lee volume specifically that modern quote sites are reprinting.

context.heading: A man with very little time saying patience is a skill
lead: Vauvenargues had reason to think hard about waiting. Born at Aix-en-Provence in 1715, he spent his twenties as an infantry officer, froze his legs during the retreat from the Siege of Prague in 1742, fought at Dettingen, and left the army with his health broken. He published one book, anonymously, in 1746 — Introduction à la connoissance de l’esprit humain, with the Réflexions and Maximes appended at the back — encouraged by Voltaire, who had been corresponding with him since 1743 and who pressed him toward a revised second edition. He died in Paris the following year, aged 31.

Read against that, the maxim is not a greetings-card sentiment. Patience as an art makes it something practised rather than possessed, and defining it by hoping rather than by endurance is the whole move: the waiting is not blank, it is aimed at something.
context.detailsSummary: Why the maxim number changes from edition to edition
detailsBody: Modern references cite this as maxim 251, and that number is stable across sources: Wikiquote gives it as no. 251, and as ‘Réflexions, CCLI’ via Hoyt’s cyclopedia ↗, while F. G. Stevens’s 1940 bilingual edition prints it between 250 and 252.

The 1746 first edition does not use that number, because it does not run one continuous sequence. Its maxims are numbered afresh inside each of three books, and this one stands as no. CV of the third, after “La nécessité comble les maux qu’elle ne peut soulager” and before the maxim on silence and reflection. Later collected editions renumbered the whole run straight through, which is where 251 comes from — so a citation to “maxim 251” and a citation to the 1746 book point at the same sentence.

sourcesVerified.claim: The 1746 Briasson first edition of Introduction à la connoissance de l'esprit humain, suivie de Réflexions et de Maximes contains "La patience est l'art d'espérer." among the numbered maxims of its third book (OCR of the long-s text reads "La patience eftl'art d'efperer", sitting between numbers CIV and CVI, after "Fin du second Livre / LIVRE III").
Elizabeth Lee's 1903 translation (Westminster: Archibald Constable & Co.) contains "Patience is the art of hoping." on page 180, between the maxims on the favourites of fortune and on despair.

F. G. Stevens's 1940 bilingual edition (London: Humphrey Milford) prints "La patience est l'art d'espérer." and "Patience is the art of hoping." positioned between maxims 250 and 252, i.e. as no. 251; its prefatory note states the text follows Pierre Varillon's edition and excludes 245 maxims dropped from Vauvenargues's second edition.

J. De Finod's A Thousand Flashes of French Wit, Wisdom, and Wickedness (New York: D. Appleton and Company, 1880 — imprint year printed on the title page) contains "Patience is the art of hoping." on p. 106, credited to "Vauvenargues" (OCR reads "Vauvenargtus") — i.e. the identical four-word English sentence 23 years before Lee's 1903 volume.
Wikiquote's Vauvenargues page lists "Patience is the art of hoping." under Reflections and Maxims (1746) with the French original and the citation "Tr. E. Lee (1903) p. 180".
Wikiquote's Patience page cites the line as Marquis de Vauvenargues, Reflections and Maxims (1746) no. 251, and also as "Réflexions, CCLI" via Hoyt's New Cyclopedia of Practical Quotations.

Wikipedia states Vauvenargues was born 6 August 1715 at Aix-en-Provence and died 28 May 1747 in Paris at age 31; that he served as an officer, took part in the Siege of Prague (1742) and the Battle of Dettingen; that in 1746 he anonymously published a single volume comprising Introduction à la connaissance de l'esprit humain with Reflexions and Maximes appended; that a revised second edition appeared in 1747; and that Voltaire encouraged him to publish, their correspondence beginning in April 1743.

AZQuotes credits "Patience is the art of hoping." to "Luc de Clapiers" and gives its source as the 1903 volume La Bruyère and Vauvenargues: Selections from the Characters, Reflexions and Maxims, naming no translator.
